entry.evidence: So far it remains unclear whether these differences are due to variations in warming rates in individual models or whether local feedback mechanisms

steps.action: Pose the question whether the spread in projected 21st-century ice-shelf melt under similar scenarios comes from ESM warming rates or from local surface-energy-budget feedbacks.
steps.quote: So far it remains unclear whether these differences are due to variations in warming rates in individual models

steps.action: Name two rivals: differences in ESM warming rates versus local SEB feedback mechanisms, with clouds as the candidate feedback.
steps.quote: [...] energy budget could also play a notable role

steps.action: Take the phenomenon, a melt spread at equal warming in MAR projections, from earlier work (Kittel et al. 2021; Gilbert and Kittel 2021).
steps.quote: projected melt changes can vary considerably even at the same rate of warming

steps.action: Design the study as dynamical downscaling of four CMIP5/CMIP6 ESMs with MAR under RCP8.5/SSP5-8.5, then attribute melt differences across SEB components.
steps.quote: with four ESMs from the CMIP5 (ACCESS1.3 and NorESM1-M) and CMIP6 (CNRM-CM6-1, CESM2) database using the highest-greenhouse-gas-concentration pathways

steps.action: Check the MAR premise: cite prior evaluations against weather stations and satellites, and run a first comparison of liquid and ice water path against CloudSat–CALIPSO (Figs. S1, S2).
steps.quote: suggests that MAR underestimates the liquid water path (LWP; Fig. S1)

steps.action: Protect the attribution from the LWP/IWP bias by arguing that a bias shared by all downscalings cancels in comparisons between experiments.
steps.quote: this bias affects all simulations in an equivalent way, and its influence is likely removed in comparisons between different downscalings of ESMs

steps.action: Simplify the SEB to the four atmospheric fluxes, restrict the analysis to summer (DJF) anomalies relative to 1981–2010, and define ESM warming over 90–60° S.
steps.quote: We neglect snow thermal diffusion and liquid water refreezing energy as the focus of this study is on the atmospheric factors

steps.action: Run (or reuse) MAR projections at 35 km over 1975–2100 forced by the four ESMs; their evaluation is in Kittel et al. (2021).
steps.quote: We performed our projections with MAR using a 35 km spatial resolution over 1975–2100

steps.action: Quantify the spread in cumulative summer melt across the four forcings: a factor of about 3.9, from about 7600 to 30 150 Gt.
steps.quote: We find a factor of ∼ 3.9 between the lowest and highest cumulative melt changes over the 21st century

steps.action: Decompose melt and SEB changes by region (AP, EAIS, WAIS) and compare melt against ESM warming (Fig. 2); identify the WAIS and LWN as the source of spread at equal warming.
steps.quote: However, only LWN is projected to strongly increase and explains uncertainties in melt.

steps.action: Exclude warming rate (ECS, regional warming) as the sole explanation, because CNRM-CM6-1 melts more than the others at the same warming.
steps.quote: This highlights that other local physical mechanisms have to be involved in addition to ESM warming rates to explain the spread

steps.action: State the rival drivers of the LWD differences over the WAIS: atmospheric temperature, water vapour, and cloud properties (greenhouse forcing held equal by scenario design).
steps.quote: We therefore analyse the contribution of the remaining factors – atmospheric temperature, water vapour, and cloud properties.

steps.action: Compute the maximal LWD contribution of atmospheric temperature by treating the atmosphere as a longwave-opaque black body (Sect. S4, Table S1).
steps.quote: Approximating the atmosphere as a longwave-opaque and black body (see Sect. S4), we estimated the maximal potential contribution of the atmospheric temperature

steps.action: Exclude temperature (at most 31 % of the CESM2–CNRM-CM6-1 LWD difference) and water vapour (similar Clausius–Clapeyron increases) as the cause of the spread at equal warming.
steps.quote: could not explain more than 31 % of modelled future LWD differences

steps.action: Compare cloud cover and cloud optical depth changes across experiments at equal warming (Figs. 3c, 4); CNRM-CM6-1 has the largest increases.
steps.quote: MAR driven by CNRM-CM6-1 simulates stronger changes in COD than other experiments for equivalent near-surface warming rates over the ice shelves

steps.action: Fit exponential LWD–COD relations per experiment (R2 ≈ 0.98–0.99) and infer that LWD stays sensitive to COD through 2100.
steps.quote: The relations expressed in Fig. suggest that the sensitivity of the LWD increase would progressively stop

steps.action: Compare IWP and LWP changes across experiments (Figs. 6, 7); larger LWP increases in CNRM-CM6-1 control the LWD spread at equal warming.
steps.quote: The different increases in LWP control the spread in projected LWD for the same warming rate.

steps.action: Refine the phase claim with a mechanism: boundary humidity profiles show low-level moisture advection in CNRM-CM6-1 (droplets) versus mid/high-level advection in CESM2 (snow) (Fig. 8, Table S2, Figs. S5–S6).
steps.quote: low-level humidity advection, where the temperature is higher, leads to the formation of more water droplets in the CNRM-CM6-1 experiment

steps.action: Compare albedo decrease against ESM warming (Fig. 9); CNRM-CM6-1 shows a stronger albedo decrease over the WAIS, linked to its cloud-driven melt.
steps.quote: MAR forced by CNRM-CM6-1 projects a stronger albedo decrease over the WAIS sector associated with large warming rates

steps.action: Run a sensitivity experiment with rainfall set to zero in the CNRM-CM6-1 simulation to test whether liquid precipitation amplifies the albedo decrease.
steps.quote: a sensitivity experiment in MAR forced by CNRM-CM6-1 where rainfall amounts were set to 0 reveals no difference

steps.action: Exclude a rain–albedo contribution to melt differences, within the precipitation rates projected.
steps.quote: differences in liquid precipitation due to clouds do not further strengthen melt differences

steps.action: Propose that in warmer climates with lower albedo the summer cloud radiative effect could reverse, as over the Greenland ablation zone.
steps.quote: These warmer conditions could reverse the summer cloud radiative effect, reducing melt

steps.action: Keep the claim that cloud water content and phase, mainly through LWN and the melt–albedo feedback, explain melt differences at a given warming.
steps.quote: we highlight the importance of cloud water content and phase to explain the differences in projected melt for a given warming

steps.action: Restrict the claim to clouds as simulated in MAR, state that no projection is more plausible than another, and name drifting snow and the LWP bias as limits.
steps.quote: clouds and their phase as simulated in MAR are important factors contributing to the spread in melt

sequences.source_document: Open discussion of tc-2021-263 (RC1, AC1, RC2, AC2, RC3, AC3)

steps.action: Asked for a full present-day melt and cloud-condition evaluation (RC1 ¶5); the authors declined it as beyond scope.
steps.quote: we think that a detailed evaluation as done in King et al. (2015) or Gilbert et al. (2020) is beyond the scope of our manuscript

steps.action: Compared MAR daily melt with Jakobs et al. (2020) at several AWS, and melt and albedo at AWS17 against cloud cover (Figs. R1–R3); not carried into the published text.
steps.quote: However, we provide a “raw” daily comparison as suggested by the reviewer

steps.action: Compared MAR summer IWP and LWP with CloudSat–CALIPSO over 2010–2016 (Figs. R4, R5); this became Figs. S1–S2 and the §2.1 ¶2 text.
steps.quote: We provide a comparison of the mean summer IWP (Fig. R4) and LWP (Fig. R5) from Cloudsat-Calipso and MAR over 2010–2016

steps.action: Defended the attribution against the cloud bias: a bias common to all runs is damped in differences between downscalings.
steps.quote: it affects all simulations in an equivalent way, and its influence is likely damped when looking at differences betweens different downscallings of ESM

steps.action: Ran surface-scheme sensitivity experiments over 2094–2100 with CNRM-CM6-1: rain set to 0, and 25 % or 50 % of snow converted to rain.
steps.quote: We set rain to 0 (SS (RF=0)) or convert a fraction of snow into rain

steps.action: Excluded the rain–albedo feedback as a source of melt differences; the published §3.3 reports only the rain-zero run.
steps.quote: The theoretical development and the sensitivity experiments suggest that differences in rain do not contribute to differences in melt.

steps.action: Redid the whole analysis per region (AP, EAIS, WAIS); this moved the focus of the attribution to the West Antarctic ice shelves.
steps.quote: As also requested by Reviewer #2, we present the same analysis but per regions together with maps.

steps.action: To check whether the differences come from forcing or from MAR, compared ESM humidity changes at 850 and 500 hPa (Figs. R11, R12), later supplement maps.
steps.quote: we have compared the humidity change at 850 hPa (Fig. R11) and 500 hPa (Fig. R12) projected by the ESMs

steps.action: Asked to compare ESM cloud fields themselves; declined because the outputs were not downloaded and CESM2 is no longer available.
steps.quote: we did not download these ESM outputs from the ESGF nodes

steps.action: Narrowed the conclusion from 'improve cloud representation in climate models' to clouds 'as simulated in MAR', and added the MAR LWP bias.
steps.quote: we suggest that clouds and their phase as simulated in MAR are important factors

steps.action: Asked to replace cumulative melt and fluxes with averages or SLR equivalents; declined, keeping cumulative values.
steps.quote: We use cumulative numbers as they highlight the total melt production over a century.

steps.action: Asked for planetary boundary layer heights in East Antarctica; declined because PBL height was not saved.
steps.quote: Unfortunately we did not save the height of the PBL in our simulations

steps.action: Added albedo-difference analysis (published as Fig. 9 and §3.3) in response to the request for a rigorous account of albedo.
steps.quote: we acknowledge that a map with albedo differences will contribute to improve our manuscript and will therefore be added

steps.action: Asked to demonstrate LWD saturation at large COD; extended the exponential fits (Fig. R13), judged the extrapolated thresholds arbitrary, and dropped the numerical saturation values.
steps.quote: are based on the strong extrapolation of an exponential function that is likely very uncertain

steps.action: Computed the share of summer melt from days above the 95th percentile, present versus future (Figs. R14, R15); proposed for §3.1 but absent from the published text.
steps.quote: We compared the amount of mean melt produced during the strongest events (daily melt above the p95 of the climate period)

tree.answer: Large spread in projected ice-shelf melt under equivalent forcing, even at equal warming
No; the phenomenon exists only in model projections (MAR downscaling of ESMs)
Explain the physical SEB drivers of the melt spread
ESM warming rate/ECS; atmospheric temperature; water vapour; cloud cover, COD and phase; rain–albedo feedback
Partly: black-body bound on the temperature contribution; Clausius–Clapeyron for water vapour; comparison at equal warming
Set in the model: choice of ESM forcings, comparison at equal warming, one rain-zero sensitivity run
Partly: rain-off sensitivity run and regional consistency; MAR physics never varied; single RCM
Cloud liquid water (LWP) drives the melt spread at equal warming via LWD and the melt–albedo feedback, as simulated in MAR
Survived with added CloudSat comparison, regional analysis and rain experiments; claim narrowed to 'as simulated in MAR'

end.claim: For the same warming rate, differences in projected summer ice-shelf melt in MAR arise mainly from cloud properties, especially more liquid-containing clouds that raise LWD and trigger the melt–albedo feedback; ESM warming still controls absolute melt differences.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing LWP and IWP changes between CNRM-CM6-1 and CESM2 at equal warming shows that larger LWP increases control the LWD spread; without this comparison the cloud-phase claim would not exist.

gates.evidence: The projections appear to be the experiments already evaluated in Kittel et al. (2021) ('The evaluation of these MAR experiments can be found in'), so no hypothesis directed their acquisition. Only the rain-zero sensitivity run was hypothesis-directed, and the review file shows it was prompted by referees. The temperature rival faced a black-body bound it could have passed (§3.2.1 ¶1), but the cloud-phase claim was never tested against observations of future change or against varied MAR physics. Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Black-body approximation of a longwave-opaque atmosphere to bound the temperature contribution to LWD
Clausius–Clapeyron relation for water vapour increase with warming
Exponential regression with determination coefficient for LWD versus COD

limits: The paper's evidence is internal to one regional model (MAR v3.11) forced by four ESMs. The cloud-phase attribution is a best explanation among the stated rivals, not a decisive test. MAR cloud physics was not varied, and the ESM cloud fields were never compared; the review shows they were unavailable. Inference: the projections were reused from Kittel et al. (2021) rather than run for this question, so the sequence is analysis-first and the S step is coded as inherited. The CloudSat–CALIPSO comparison is a first, uncorrected look reported only in the supplement; the authors acknowledge an LWP underestimate and protect the claim by assuming the bias cancels in differences, which is not tested. Several review-forced analyses do not appear in the published text: daily melt against Jakobs et al. (2020), the 25 %/50 % snow-to-rain experiments, and the melt-event ratio (§3.1 does not contain it). The published §3.3 cites only the rain-zero run. The regional (WAIS) focus was introduced in response to referees. Sub-claims at other statuses: the humidity-advection mechanism (§3.2.3 ¶3) is best_explanation; the LWD–COD saturation (§3.2.2 ¶3) is regularity_in_range within the simulated COD range, with the extrapolated thresholds removed after review; the absence of a rain–albedo contribution (§3.3 ¶2) holds only for the projected precipitation rates; the possible future reversal of the cloud radiative effect (§3.3 ¶3) is an untested hypothesis. Drifting snow is not modelled.

disagreements.target: Temperature-based diagnostics of Antarctic melt (Trusel et al., 2015)
disagreements.support: MAR projections show melt changes that differ by up to a factor of about 1.6 over the WAIS between CNRM-CM6-1 and CESM2 at similar warming.
disagreements.quote: While melt amounts can be determined from a temperature-based diagnostic , projected melt changes can vary considerably even at the same rate of warming

disagreements.target: Common practice of assessing Antarctic SLR contribution at specific warming levels (e.g. Pattyn et al., 2018)
disagreements.support: Liquid-containing clouds produce large melt and hydrofracture-vulnerability differences between CNRM-CM6-1 and CESM2 at a similar warming rate.
disagreements.quote: liquid-containing clouds could lead to large uncertainties even for the same warming rate

disagreements.target: ECS as the measure of ESM warming sensitivity explaining melt differences (Zelinka et al., 2020)
disagreements.support: CNRM-CM6-1 (ECS 4.9) yields more melt than CESM2 (ECS 5.15), and still more at equal regional warming (Fig. 2).
disagreements.quote: Nonetheless, ECS does not wholly explain the differences between the CESM2 (ECS of 5.15) and CNRM-CM6-1 (ECS of 4.9) experiments
